lessons.title: Specific heat capacity and latent heat

lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Define and use specific heat capacity (Q = mcΔθ) and specific latent heat (Q = mL)
Solve problems on heating, melting, boiling and mixing, including electrical heating
Interpret a heating curve and explain why temperature stays constant during a change of state
reviewNotes: c = 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, L_f = 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹, L_v = 2.26 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹ are textbook values; the board's data sheet may round differently (e.g. 4180, 3.3 × 10⁵).
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Heat capacities and latent heats
blocks.md:
The **specific heat capacity** c of a substance is the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg by 1 K: **Q = mcΔθ** (J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹). For water c ≈ 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. The **heat capacity** of a body is C = mc (J K⁻¹).

The **specific latent heat** L is the energy needed to change the state of 1 kg without a change of temperature: **Q = mL**. For ice L_f ≈ 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹ (fusion) and for water L_v ≈ 2.26 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹ (vaporisation).

blocks.title: Method
blocks.md:
1. Split the process into stages: heating a solid, melting, heating the liquid, boiling, heating the vapour.
2. Use mcΔθ for the stages with a temperature change and mL for the changes of state.
3. Add the energies. For mixing: heat lost by the hot body = heat gained by the cold body (no losses).
4. For electrical heating: Pt = mcΔθ (+ losses). Efficiency = useful energy ÷ energy supplied.

blocks.caption: Heating curve of ice to steam (schematic, not to scale).
blocks.alt: Temperature against energy supplied: ice warming, a flat melting stage at 0 degrees, water warming, a flat boiling stage at 100 degrees, then steam warming.

blocks.title: Why the temperature is constant at a change of state
blocks.md: During melting or boiling the energy supplied increases the **potential energy** of the molecules (their separation) and not their mean kinetic energy, so the temperature does not rise. Latent heat of vaporisation is much larger than that of fusion because the molecules must be separated completely.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Forgetting the latent heat stage (heating ice at 0 °C to water at 20 °C also needs the energy to melt it).
- Using Δθ in kelvin and in °C inconsistently: a **change** of 1 K = a change of 1 °C, but absolute temperatures differ by 273.
- Mixing J and kJ, or g and kg (c is per kilogram).
- In mixing problems, forgetting that the final temperature lies between the two initial ones.

lessons.title: Ideal gases and kinetic theory
lessons.programRef: GCE Advanced Level Physics — thermal physics (to be checked against the official syllabus)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: State the gas laws and use pV = nRT and pV = NkT with temperatures in kelvin
State the assumptions of the kinetic theory and use p = ⅓ρ⟨c²⟩ to relate pressure to molecular motion
Relate mean molecular kinetic energy to absolute temperature: ½m⟨c²⟩ = (3/2)kT
reviewNotes: R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹, N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ and T = θ + 273 are used.
The derivation of p = ⅓ρ⟨c²⟩ is stated, not derived; check whether the board expects the derivation.
Real gases and Van der Waals are not included.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: The ideal gas
blocks.md:
An **ideal gas** obeys **pV = nRT** exactly (n in mol, T in K, R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹); in terms of the number of molecules N: **pV = NkT** (k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹ = R/N_A, N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹).

Special cases: Boyle (T constant) pV = constant; pressure law (V constant) p/T = constant; Charles (p constant) V/T = constant. **T (K) = θ (°C) + 273**.

blocks.title: Kinetic theory of gases
blocks.md:
Assumptions: many identical molecules in random motion; negligible volume compared with the container; no intermolecular forces except during (elastic) collisions; collision time negligible.

Result: **pV = ⅓Nm⟨c²⟩**, i.e. p = ⅓ρ⟨c²⟩. Comparing with pV = NkT: **½m⟨c²⟩ = (3/2)kT**. The r.m.s. speed is c_rms = √⟨c²⟩ = √(3RT/M) (M = molar mass in kg mol⁻¹).

blocks.caption: Isotherms of an ideal gas: pV = constant at each temperature.
blocks.alt: Two hyperbola-shaped curves of pressure against volume, the upper one for a higher temperature.

blocks.title: Internal energy
blocks.md: For an ideal gas the internal energy is the total kinetic energy of the molecules (no potential energy): for a monatomic gas **U = (3/2)nRT**. It depends only on temperature. A real gas behaves ideally at low pressure and high temperature.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Using °C instead of kelvin in gas-law calculations (always add 273).
- Using g mol⁻¹ instead of kg mol⁻¹ for M in c_rms.
- Using volume in dm³ or cm³ with R in SI: convert to m³ (1 dm³ = 10⁻³ m³).
- Writing ⟨c²⟩ as (⟨c⟩)²: the mean of the squares is larger.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Amount of gas
blocks.statement: A cylinder of volume 25 dm³ holds an ideal gas at 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa and 27 °C. Find the number of moles and molecules.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Speed of molecules
blocks.statement: Find the r.m.s. speed of nitrogen molecules (M = 0.028 kg mol⁻¹) at 300 K and the mean kinetic energy of a molecule.
